title: What The World Is Today
theme: The urban soul humanism of the early 1970s — records that bore witness to city life, community struggle, and the human cost of a world in flux, from the streets of Harlem to the mines of West Virginia.
narrativePurpose: Test knowledge of the socially conscious soul records that defined 1970–1975 — the songs, albums, labels, songwriters, and biographical facts behind the artists who made R&B a vehicle for truth-telling about American life.
toneProgression: Identify the record and the artist → labels, songwriters, producers, and chart facts → birth names, birthplaces, and the hidden connections that deepen the story

vault.note: Digit 4 (index 3) is always visible. Vault code 1-9-7-2 — the episode's densest year: Bobby Womack's 'Across 110th Street,' The Stylistics' 'People Make The World Go Round,' Curtis Mayfield's 'Freddie's Dead,' and Donny Hathaway's Live — featuring 'Little Ghetto Boy' — all arrived in 1972. The year socially conscious soul found its fullest voice.

questions.question: Stevie Wonder's 'Living For The City' — a seven-minute portrait of urban disillusionment — appeared on which 1973 album?
choices: Songs in the Key of Life

metadata.fact: 'Living For The City' appeared on Innervisions (1973) — one of Stevie Wonder's masterworks from his celebrated mid-70s run of creative freedom. The track's seven-minute runtime included a spoken-word scene in which a young Southern man arrives in New York City and is immediately swept into the criminal justice system.
metadata.storyHook: Seven minutes. One story. A young man arrives in New York City and never gets the chance he was promised. Stevie Wonder put the whole thing on Innervisions.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Stevie Wonder 'Living For The City' from Innervisions (1973), Tamla/Motown. Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: 'Midnight Train to Georgia' by Gladys Knight & The Pips was originally written by Jim Weatherly under which different title?

metadata.fact: Jim Weatherly originally wrote and recorded 'Midnight Plane to Houston' on Amos Records. Gladys Knight heard the song and asked Weatherly to change the title — replacing the plane with a train and the destination with Georgia. The retitled version became one of the era's most celebrated R&B records.
metadata.storyHook: It was a plane. It was going to Houston. Gladys Knight asked for a train to Georgia instead — and Jim Weatherly rewrote his own song for her.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: 'Midnight Train to Georgia' originally 'Midnight Plane to Houston' by Jim Weatherly on Amos Records. Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: 'Ball of Confusion (That's What The World Is Today)' was a 1970 political soul anthem by which Motown group?

metadata.song: Ball of Confusion (That's What The World Is Today)
metadata.fact: 'Ball of Confusion' was produced by Norman Whitfield and written by Whitfield and Barrett Strong for The Temptations in 1970 — part of the group's psychedelic soul era that transformed their sound from smooth harmonies to socially charged, studio-experimental R&B.
metadata.storyHook: The Temptations in 1970 sounded nothing like the Temptations of 1965. Norman Whitfield changed everything — and 'Ball of Confusion' was the proof.

questions.question: 'Grandma's Hands' appeared on which 1971 Bill Withers debut album?

metadata.fact: Just As I Am (1971) was Bill Withers's debut studio album on Sussex Records — produced by Booker T. Jones. It introduced both 'Ain't No Sunshine' and 'Grandma's Hands' to the world in the same release, making it one of the most remarkable debut albums in R&B history.
metadata.storyHook: 'Ain't No Sunshine' and 'Grandma's Hands' on the same debut album. Bill Withers arrived with more fully formed material than most artists manage in a career.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Bill Withers Just As I Am (1971), Sussex Records, Booker T. Jones producer, debut album. Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: 'People Make The World Go Round' was a 1972 social commentary hit for which Philadelphia vocal group?

metadata.song: People Make The World Go Round
topicTags: People Make The World Go Round
metadata.fact: 'People Make The World Go Round' appeared on The Stylistics' debut album and was one of the group's more explicitly socially conscious records — a departure from the pure romantic balladry they were known for. Produced by Thom Bell and released on Avco Records, it demonstrated that Philadelphia soul could carry political weight as well as emotional weight.
metadata.storyHook: The Stylistics were known for love songs. 'People Make The World Go Round' proved they could do something harder — and they did it without losing the melody.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: The Stylistics 'People Make The World Go Round' (1972), Avco Records, Thom Bell production. Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: William DeVaughn's 'Be Thankful For What You Got' was released on which independent label?

metadata.song: Be Thankful For What You Got
metadata.album: Be Thankful for What You Got
topicTags: Be Thankful For What You Got
metadata.fact: 'Be Thankful For What You Got' was released on Roxbury Records — a subsidiary of Chelsea Records — and became one of the era's most remarkable independent soul success stories, reaching #1 on both the Billboard Hot 100 and the R&B chart in 1974. DeVaughn's quiet, deliberate delivery gave the record an unhurried dignity that perfectly matched its message.
metadata.storyHook: An independent label. A message about gratitude. Number one on the Hot 100 and the R&B chart. William DeVaughn did it without a major label behind him.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: William DeVaughn 'Be Thankful For What You Got' on Roxbury Records (1974), #1 Hot 100 and R&B. Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: 'Wake Up Everybody' featured which vocalist in the lead role — a singer who would soon become one of Philadelphia soul's defining solo stars?

metadata.fact: Teddy Pendergrass was the lead vocalist on 'Wake Up Everybody' — still a member of Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes when the record was released in 1975. He would leave the group the following year to launch a solo career that made him one of Philadelphia soul's most powerful voices of the late 1970s.
metadata.storyHook: He was still in the group. He was already the reason people listened. Teddy Pendergrass made 'Wake Up Everybody' sound like a solo record — and then he made that official.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Teddy Pendergrass lead vocalist on Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes 'Wake Up Everybody' (1975), Philadelphia International Records. Must be sourced before production.

reserve.question: 'The Ghetto' and 'Little Ghetto Boy' were both recorded by which artist — one of early 70s soul's most gifted and tragic figures?

metadata.fact: Donny Hathaway recorded both 'The Ghetto' (1970, from Everything Is Everything) and 'Little Ghetto Boy' (featured on Live, 1972) — two of early 70s soul's most unsparing portraits of urban poverty. Hathaway's extraordinary vocal and musical gifts gave both records an emotional precision that few contemporaries matched.
metadata.storyHook: The Ghetto. Little Ghetto Boy. Two records. Same artist. Donny Hathaway returned to the same subject twice — and both times he said something nobody else could.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Donny Hathaway 'The Ghetto' from Everything Is Everything (1970); 'Little Ghetto Boy' from Live (1972). Must be sourced before production.

reserve.question: 'Across 110th Street' was written and performed by which artist for the 1972 film of the same name?

metadata.fact: 'Across 110th Street' was written and performed by Bobby Womack for the 1972 blaxploitation film of the same name — set in Harlem and directed by Barry Shear. The song's gritty, string-drenched opening became one of the most recognizable moments in soul cinema history.
metadata.storyHook: Harlem. 1972. A film about the streets above 110th Street. Bobby Womack wrote the title track — and it became the sound of an entire era of urban cinema.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Bobby Womack 'Across 110th Street' from the 1972 film soundtrack, United Artists Records. Must be sourced before production.

reserve.question: 'Freddie's Dead' — Curtis Mayfield's 1972 blaxploitation anthem — was written and produced by which artist?

metadata.fact: 'Freddie's Dead (Theme from Superfly)' was written, produced, and performed by Curtis Mayfield for the 1972 film Super Fly. Mayfield's decision to score a film glorifying drug culture with music that explicitly criticised it created one of the era's most striking artistic contradictions — and one of its best soundtracks.
metadata.storyHook: The film glorified the drug dealer. The music condemned him. Curtis Mayfield wrote Freddie's Dead as a critique from inside a soundtrack everyone assumed celebrated what it was actually mourning.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Curtis Mayfield 'Freddie's Dead' from Super Fly (1972), Curtom Records. Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: 'Wake Up Everybody' was co-written by Gene McFadden and John Whitehead — who later recorded which 1979 disco-soul anthem together?

metadata.fact: Gene McFadden and John Whitehead co-wrote 'Wake Up Everybody' for Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes in 1975 — and later recorded 'Ain't No Stoppin' Us Now' as McFadden & Whitehead in 1979, making them one of the era's most consistent Philadelphia soul songwriting-to-performing talents.
metadata.storyHook: They wrote 'Wake Up Everybody' in 1975. Four years later they recorded 'Ain't No Stoppin' Us Now' themselves. McFadden and Whitehead understood both sides of the studio.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Gene McFadden and John Whitehead co-wrote 'Wake Up Everybody' (1975) and later recorded 'Ain't No Stoppin' Us Now' (1979) as McFadden & Whitehead. Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: 'Ball of Confusion' was produced by Norman Whitfield and co-written by Whitfield alongside which Motown lyricist — the pair's frequent creative partner?

metadata.fact: Barrett Strong co-wrote 'Ball of Confusion' alongside Norman Whitfield — a partnership that had already produced 'I Heard It Through the Grapevine' for Marvin Gaye. Strong's lyrical directness combined with Whitfield's dense, experimental production gave the record its political weight.
metadata.storyHook: Barrett Strong and Norman Whitfield. The same team that wrote 'I Heard It Through the Grapevine' applied their gifts to the state of the world — and 'Ball of Confusion' was the result.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: 'Ball of Confusion' co-written by Norman Whitfield and Barrett Strong (1970). Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: Gladys Knight & The Pips released 'Midnight Train to Georgia' on which label — after departing from Motown?

metadata.fact: Gladys Knight & The Pips left Motown and signed with Buddah Records — releasing 'Midnight Train to Georgia' and their acclaimed album Imagination in 1973. The move from Motown to an independent label proved commercially inspired: the Buddah recordings became their most celebrated work.
metadata.storyHook: They left Motown. They signed with Buddah. They made 'Midnight Train to Georgia.' Sometimes leaving is the right decision.

questions.question: Donny Hathaway's 'The Ghetto' (1970) was co-written with which artist — who later replaced Curtis Mayfield as lead singer of The Impressions?

metadata.fact: Leroy Hutson co-wrote 'The Ghetto' with Donny Hathaway — the two had been college roommates at Howard University. Hutson later replaced Curtis Mayfield as lead singer of The Impressions when Mayfield departed for his solo career, connecting two of early 70s soul's most important creative circles.
metadata.storyHook: College roommates. Co-writers. One replaced Curtis Mayfield. The other became Donny Hathaway. Leroy Hutson and Donny Hathaway shared a dorm room — and changed soul music.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Leroy Hutson co-wrote 'The Ghetto' with Donny Hathaway (college roommates at Howard University); Hutson replaced Curtis Mayfield in The Impressions. Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: 'Grandma's Hands' was produced by which Booker T. & the M.G.'s frontman — whose production gave Bill Withers's debut its warm, sparse sound?

metadata.fact: Booker T. Jones — organist and leader of Booker T. & the M.G.'s — produced Just As I Am, Bill Withers's debut album. His approach to the record matched Withers's own instincts: spare, warm, and rooted in the space between the notes rather than the density of arrangement.
metadata.storyHook: Booker T. Jones produced it. Bill Withers wrote it. The combination gave 'Grandma's Hands' a sound that felt like it had always existed — even on first listen.

reserve.question: 'Little Ghetto Boy' by Donny Hathaway appears on which 1972 live album?

questions.question: Bill Withers — who recorded 'Grandma's Hands' about his grandmother's life — was born in which tiny West Virginia mining town?

metadata.fact: Bill Withers was born on July 4, 1938, in Slab Fork, West Virginia — a small coal mining community. He worked as an aircraft parts installer for the Navy before his music career began, and the working-class roots he carried from Slab Fork shaped every record he made.
metadata.storyHook: Slab Fork, West Virginia. A coal mining town. The place that made Bill Withers who he was — and 'Grandma's Hands' was his way of putting it on record.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Bill Withers born Slab Fork, West Virginia. Must be sourced before production.

questions.question: Stevie Wonder — who recorded 'Living For The City' — was born under which full legal name?

metadata.fact: Stevie Wonder was born Stevland Hardaway Morris on May 13, 1950, in Saginaw, Michigan. He was signed to Motown's Tamla imprint as a child and performed as 'Little Stevie Wonder' before transitioning to his adult creative peak in the early 1970s.
metadata.storyHook: Stevland Hardaway Morris. Born blind in Saginaw, Michigan. Signed to Motown as a child. By 1973 he was making Innervisions — and nobody was calling him Little Stevie Wonder anymore.
metadata.sourceNotes: PRIORITY VERIFY: Stevie Wonder born Stevland Hardaway Morris, Saginaw, Michigan. Must be sourced before production.

metadata.fact: Jim Weatherly originally released 'Midnight Plane to Houston' on Amos Records — before Gladys Knight heard it and asked him to change the title. metadata.album: Be Thankful for What You Got
metadata.fact: William DeVaughn was from the Washington D.C. metropolitan area — specifically from the Maryland suburbs. metadata.storyHook: Maryland. The D.C. suburbs. Not a city associated with soul music's commercial peaks. But that's where William DeVaughn came from — and 'Be Thankful For What You Got' went to number one anyway.
